Why America’s Semiconductor Manufacturing Capacity Mattersby Daniel Nenni on 10-21-2026 at 8:00 am

View Articles

Categories: Intel Foundry, Semiconductor2 Comments

Key takeaways ▼

America’s semiconductor future will be shaped by its ability to turn scientific discoveries into chips manufactured at scale. That is why the investments outlined in Intel Foundry’s recent editorial matter beyond the company’s own business. They address a fundamental question: whether the United States can sustain the research, industrial infrastructure and skilled workforce needed to help define the next era of computing. As artificial intelligence and other demanding applications expand, the ability to manufacture advanced semiconductors becomes a foundation for economic opportunity, technological leadership and national resilience.
The editorial highlights the scale of the challenge. Citing the Semiconductor Industry Association, it notes that America’s share of global semiconductor manufacturing fell from 37% in 1990 to 10% in 2022. That decline matters because chips support essential systems, from communications and transportation to health care and industrial equipment. Concentrating manufacturing capacity in fewer locations creates exposure to disruptions. Expanding domestic production can give businesses more sourcing options and help strengthen continuity for industries that depend on reliable access to computing technology.
Perhaps the editorial’s most consequential argument is that manufacturing and innovation reinforce each other. Developing a breakthrough transistor or packaging technology is only part of the work. Engineers must also learn how to produce it consistently, economically and in enormous volumes. Keeping research, development and manufacturing closely connected allows lessons from the factory to inform the next design. Over time, that exchange builds expertise that is difficult to replicate. When production moves away, a country risks losing some of the practical knowledge that helps generate its next breakthrough.
An American flag hangs from Intel’s Fab 62 in Arizona, where construction continues on the company’s sixth high-volume manufacturing facility at Ocotillo. (Credit: Intel Corporation)
Intel presents its advanced process and packaging technologies as examples of this connection. Their broader significance lies in the capabilities they represent: finding new ways to improve performance, manage power and connect increasingly complex systems. Progress in computing depends on advances across these areas. A domestic ecosystem that can develop and manufacture them gives American researchers and businesses a stronger platform for pursuing future applications. It also creates more opportunities for collaboration among chip designers, equipment providers, materials specialists and manufacturers.
The construction updates make that ambition tangible. Intel says construction and tool installation are underway at Arizona’s Fab 62, with operations expected by the end of 2028, while its Ohio project has reached another structural milestone. These developments matter because semiconductor capacity takes years to establish. Buildings, specialized equipment, utilities and trained teams must come together before a facility can deliver useful output. Construction progress therefore signals preparation for future demand, although the eventual impact will depend on execution, customer adoption and competitive manufacturing performance.
The economic reach also extends well beyond the factory gate. According to the editorial, Intel works with more than 4,500 suppliers across 49 states and generates more than $29 billion in annual domestic spending. Those relationships show how semiconductor investment can support businesses providing equipment, materials, construction and specialized services. For communities, the opportunity includes technical careers and stronger connections between employers and educational institutions. Realizing those benefits requires sustained workforce development, along with the housing, transportation, energy and water infrastructure needed to support industrial growth.
This matters because technological leadership requires the capacity to deliver. Announcing discoveries and building facilities are important steps, but success means translating them into reliable products that customers choose. Intel’s editorial describes an effort to strengthen the entire chain, from research through advanced packaging and high volume production. If that effort succeeds, its value will extend beyond one company’s balance sheet. It could deepen America’s industrial knowledge, expand skilled employment and give the country greater capacity to respond to technological change.
Bottom line: The central issue is whether America can keep creating the conditions that allow innovation to become something the world can use. That makes manufacturing capacity a measure of future possibility: the tools, talent and infrastructure available when the next major computing challenge arrives, and the ability to meet it with technologies developed and produced at meaningful scale.
